source.title: Are there any 'object detectors' in the hidden layers of CNNs trained to identify objects or scenes?
source.authors: Ella M. Gale; Nicholas Martin; Ryan Blything; Anh Nguyen; Jeffrey S. Bowers

record.tranche_reason: The study tests single-unit object selectivity and argues that common selectivity measures can overstate it; its own results refine claims about object detectors and show strong dependence on the measure used.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own unit-selectivity measures and human judgments of activation-maximization images. It does not identify whether the broad activations share a feature the network uses. Results cited from other studies, including ablation results, are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study does not measure polysemanticity as such, meaning responses to unrelated features. It measures whether hidden CNN units are class-selective 'object detectors'. It bears on V7 directly: the same units look highly selective under top-activation measures (precision over the top 60 images, Network Dissection IoU) or CCMAS, but poorly selective under full-range signal-detection measures. So whether a unit counts as a single-concept unit depends on the activation range examined and the scoring used. Low class selectivity does not show that units respond to unrelated inputs, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that selectivity measures disagree, and that precision, CCMAS and Network Dissection overstate selectivity. Signal-detection measures show poor hit or false-alarm rates, and the CNNs do not learn object detectors in hidden layers. They add that units respond to unknown features weakly correlated with object categories.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares several quantitative and human-interpretation measures of unit selectivity rather than reproducing either original source's method.
record.method_sensitivity: Selectivity conclusions depend strongly on the measure used and, for fc6.1199, on the activation threshold. Human interpretability of activation-maximization panels also differs by layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Hidden units in AlexNet, VGG-16 and GoogLeNet labelled 'object detectors' have high false-alarm rates (minimum 0.96 at maximum informedness) and low recall. Authors say they respond to unknown features weakly correlated with a class.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden units in image CNNs are not class-selective object detectors when judged by full-range signal-detection measures.

record.problems: The study analyzes only correctly classified images in its main AlexNet dataset and samples about 90% of conv5 units and roughly 60% of fc6 and fc7 units due to time constraints. For VGG-16 and GoogLeNet it tests selected Network Dissection bus units, not all units. The study does not directly test unrelated-input mixtures or identify shared features behind responses.
record.rows_left_out: The appendix reports many individual bus-unit measurements for VGG-16 and GoogLeNet in Tables A3-A5. These numerous per-unit table entries are not individually extracted here; the paper's highlighted Figure 6 units and main textual conclusions are recorded in R17-R19.

untested.parts: Whether units respond to several unrelated inputs. The study shows only low class selectivity, attributed to unknown features weakly correlated with a class.
Superposition as a cause. The 'superposition catastrophe' discussed is a different, memory-related notion and is not tested here.
There is no intervention on architecture or training. The models compared (AlexNet, VGG-16, GoogLeNet) are not compared on the share of polysemantic units.
Not tested; the features driving units are left unknown.
Only class/object selectivity is examined, not explanation scoring of arbitrary features or polysemanticity judgments.

missing.what: CCMAS for the best and second-best class is nearly equal across layers (e.g., fc7.0: .813 maypole vs .808 chainsaw). This suggests apparent mixed selectivity under CCMAS, though the authors argue CCMAS is unreliable.
Top-CCMAS units have very low precision (fc7.31: CCMAS .94, precision .11; fc6.582: CCMAS .93, precision .01).
Correlations between selectivity measures are weak to moderate (0.09-0.38).
Simulated examples showing CCMAS diverging from precision (CCMAS 1 with a single active item; CCMAS .06 with precision 1).

record.verdict_notes: V1 labels are removed: low class selectivity is not the same as responding to unrelated features. The study is treated as bearing on V7 because it shows that a unit's single-concept label depends on examining the top activations versus the full range and on the scoring metric. This is arguably a related construct (class selectivity), so a reviewer could instead treat it as fits_no_version. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: It measures selectivity for object classes, not responses to explicitly paired unrelated inputs or whether such responses share a feature.
Language models and transformer MLP neurons.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
The share of polysemantic neurons, SoLU, modern convnets as an intervention, and performance costs of reducing polysemanticity.
Whether apparently mixed responses share a feature such as pose or related offshoots of one job.
The study compares selectivity measures and activation-maximization interpretation; it does not systematically vary explanation-scoring procedures beyond the measures it reports.

relation.reason: Its own results on measure dependence of unit selectivity bear on V7, though it does not measure polysemanticity directly.

tranche.reason: The study does not argue that any polysemanticity version is wrong or needs restating. Its main result, that selectivity measures disagree on the same CNN units, supports V7 in a new setting and construct (vision CNN class selectivity). The fc8 contrast is minor.

source_check.notes: The study measures class selectivity ('object detectors'), not polysemanticity, so it bears on V7 only through measure and activation-range disagreement. R7 and V7.support[5] wrongly say Table A1 gives CCMAS .93 for fc6.1199 (it gives 0.92). The false-alarm figures use the authors' usage (share of above-threshold items not in the class). The human AM experiment covered conv5, fc6 and fc8 only (not fc7). Bus-unit precision (R17-R19) uses the top 100 of a 100k ImageNet subset.

statements.correction: fc6.1199: precision .98 and CCMAS .92 in Section 4.1. Section 5 says CCMAS .93. Table A1 says CCMAS 0.92 and precision .95 (top 100 items).
statements.problem: All other numbers match the text, but the CCMAS note is wrong: Table A1 gives 0.92 for fc6.1199, not 0.93. Only Section 5 says .93.

statements.correction: fc8: 71.2% (±0.6) 'yes' responses; 59.3% (±1.6) of units with at least 80% 'yes'. Of those units, humans matched the most-active image's class 95.4% (±0.6) and the CCMAS class 94.6% (±0.7). Only human AM interpretation was compared with class measures at fc8. Table 1 contrast layers: conv5 (34.1%, 0%) and fc6 (23.3%, 18.9%); fc7 not tested.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but 59.3% is the share of units with at least 80% 'yes', not a 'yes' response rate. The 95.4%/94.6% agreement covers only consistently interpreted units. fc8 got no signal-detection measures, so 'confined to hidden layers' overreaches. fc7 was not in the human AM experiment.
Fine for this study. The ~95% agreement holds for the units with consistent human interpretation (59.3% of fc8 units).

Fine. Conv5 disagreement is shown in Fig 3, Table 1 and Section 5 rather than in R2-R10 (R2-R4 are fc7, R7-R10 fc6). The same measure pair (human AM vs class) is compared across layers only in Table 1 d-e.
Fine for this study: fc8 output-layer limit and CNN scoring dependence fit the text. The study measures class selectivity, not polysemanticity.

reader_labels.condition: The tested ImageNet-trained AlexNet units and the selected GoogLeNet/VGG-16 bus units
reader_labels.reason: Units showed some class-related activity, but the tested detector measures showed poor recall or specificity rather than strong, coherent object detection (R1, R4-R8, R17-R19). The paper did not directly test unrelated-input mixtures.

reader_labels.condition: AlexNet hidden layers and the selected units in other CNNs
reader_labels.reason: Precision, CCMAS, localist criteria, signal-detection measures, and human interpretation gave materially different assessments of selectivity (R1-R10, R11-R19).
